instrumental in bringing climate justice to the forefront of global environmental discourse, striving to ensure policies and actions are fair, inclusive and effective in addressing the complex challenges of climate change.

Impact on International Agreements and Protocols

Climate justice principles are increasingly shaping international environmental agreements by bringing equity and fairness to the forefront of global climate action.

The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, is a prime example. It marks a significant shift by attempting to lower the planet’s temperature by two degrees Celsius. It also acknowledges that developed nations, which have contributed more to global emissions, should take greater responsibility in addressing climate change.

The agreement also highlights the importance of supporting vulnerable nations through financial aid and technology transfer, addressing the climate justice principle of equitable resource distribution.

It incorporates the concept of “nationally determined contributions,” allowing countries to set their climate action plans, reflecting their capabilities and circumstances. It respects the diverse socio-economic contexts of different nations, aligning with climate justice’s call for fairness and inclusivity.

Moreover, climate justice advocacy has shifted international dialogue from a purely environmental or economic focus to one considering social and ethical dimensions. There’s a growing recognition that climate policies must address the disproportionate impacts on marginalized and vulnerable populations.

This shift is evident in increased discussions about loss and damage in climate change negotiations, recognizing that some impacts are beyond adaptation and require compensation. Moreover, 10 percent of households that produce the most emissions contribute almost half of greenhouse gas emissions. Meanwhile, the bottom half contributes between 13 and percent. 

International commitments now often include components addressing equity — such as funding for adoption in developing countries — acknowledging that those who are least responsible for climate change are often the most vulnerable.

The Role of Science and Research

Scientific research advances climate justice, providing essential data and insights to understand climate change’s unequal impacts. This research highlights vulnerable communities’ disproportionate challenges, underpinning the need for equitable climate policies.

Scientists also develop future climate models, guiding policymakers on the urgency and scale of necessary actions. These scientific findings set realistic and just targets in policies for emissions reductions, renewable energy and conservation efforts.

The collaboration between scientists and policymakers is consequential to effective climate justice policies. Scientists’ data and understanding of climate phenomena inform policymakers, who transform this knowledge into practical regulations.

An example of this synergy is the influence of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change on the Paris Agreement. However, the challenge lies in making scientific research accessible to non-experts, requiring effective communication strategies.

Increasingly, participatory research is bridging this

documents.textLong:
record rainfall in Pakistan, and heatwaves in China and Europe. These events have resulted in food insecurity, mass migrations, and significant economic losses.

The report also emphasizes the increase in undernourishment, exacerbated by hydrometeorological risks, the COVID-19 pandemic, conflicts, and prolonged violence. Hazardous climate events have also triggered new population displacements and worsened the living conditions of millions of already displaced individuals.

The report also focuses on the impact of climate change on ecosystems and the environment. Recurring natural events, such as tree flowering and bird migration, are disrupted by climate change.

To address these challenges, the WMO emphasizes the importance of strengthening early warning systems. The United Nations’ “Early Warning for All” initiative aims to address the capacity gap in early warning services to ensure the protection of every individual. Currently, around a hundred countries lack adequate meteorological services.

The WMO report was released in preparation for Earth Day 2023, highlighting the need for urgent climate action. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres calls for intensifying efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and limit the global temperature increase to 1.5°C. He also emphasizes the need for massive investments in adaptation and resilience, particularly for the most vulnerable communities and countries, which have contributed the least to this crisis, according to the UN chief.

So far China has conducted three tests of its hypersonic glide weapon. The third test was carried out in early December 2014 which was, as usual, brought to light by western media. However, the Chinese Ministry of National Defence Information Office acknowledged the test and gave out its usual statement that it is a routine process conducted within its territory and is not directed against any country. China is proceeding at a rapid phase in developing hypersonic glide weapon system as these weapons cannot be intercepted by any of the currently deployed missile defence systems.

Hypersonic weapon

China has conducted three tests of its hypersonic glide weapon in just a year which points to the rapid phase and progress it is making in developing the vehicle. There are three countries in the business of developing hypersonic weapons: the United States, China and Russia. Among these countries United States and China are taking the lead.

The speed band of weapons are being shifted from supersonic to hypersonic as speed is one parameter which has been traditionally used to defeat defences. The game of speed has been on ever since mobile warfare began. The primary reason for the increasing focus on developing hypersonic weapons is because defences are evolving to intercept weapons that can travel at supersonic speed. Speed above Mach 5 is considered to fall in the hypersonic regime.

There are two types of hypersonic weapons; the weapons with its own propulsion system like a scram or RAM jet engine, for example the X-51A uses a hydrocarbon fuel scramjet engine. The other type uses a ballistic missile booster to attain the hypersonic velocity and thereafter glide its way to its target. China has opted for the second type of hypersonic vehicle for obvious reasons; firstly, it is technologically less complex compared to self propelled (scram or RAM jet) vehicles. Secondly, China has not yet mastered the art of developing even jet engines for its fighter aircraft while hypersonic vehicles would require the technologically advanced scramjet or RAM jet engines which would take a long time to master. Third, China has already mastered ballistic missile technology and has got some experience in making manoeuvrable ballistic missile warheads which could be adopted to develop the second variety of hypersonic vehicles and moreover this method would make it quicker and still give equal effect as the self propelled vehicles.

So far China has conducted three tests of its hypersonic glide weapon. The third test was carried out in early December 2014 which was, as usual, brought to light by western media. However, the Chinese Ministry of National Defence Information Office acknowledged the test and gave out its usual statement that it is a routine process conducted within its territory and is not directed against any country. China is proceeding at a rapid phase in developing hypersonic glide weapon system as these weapons cannot be intercepted by any of the currently deployed missile defence systems.

Hypersonic weapon

China has conducted three tests of its hypersonic glide weapon in just a year which points to the rapid phase and progress it is making in developing the vehicle. There are three countries in the business of developing hypersonic weapons: the United States, China and Russia. Among these countries United States and China are taking the lead.

The speed band of weapons are being shifted from supersonic to hypersonic as speed is one parameter which has been traditionally used to defeat defences. The game of speed has been on ever since mobile warfare began. The primary reason for the increasing focus on developing hypersonic weapons is because defences are evolving to intercept weapons that can travel at supersonic speed. Speed above Mach 5 is considered to fall in the hypersonic regime.

There are two types of hypersonic weapons; the weapons with its own propulsion system like a scram or RAM jet engine, for example the X-51A uses a hydrocarbon fuel scramjet engine. The other type uses a ballistic missile booster to attain the hypersonic velocity and thereafter glide its way to its target. China has opted for the second type of hypersonic vehicle for obvious reasons; firstly, it is technologically less complex compared to self propelled (scram or RAM jet) vehicles. Secondly, China has not yet mastered the art of developing even jet engines for its fighter aircraft while hypersonic vehicles would require the technologically advanced scramjet or RAM jet engines which would take a long time to master. Third, China has already mastered ballistic missile technology and has got some experience in making manoeuvrable ballistic missile warheads which could be adopted to develop the second variety of hypersonic vehicles and moreover this method would make it quicker and still give equal effect as the self propelled vehicles.
